title: Information sheet · Mayor
body:
*Memorandum prepared for Mayor [YOUR NAME] of Potamosia, by your secretary, ahead of Wednesday’s town assembly.*

Potamosia has weighed the same three building projects for some time now and it is time to act. Each of these projects would do the city good but there is not enough money for all. The treasury holds **30 gold coins**, which is enough for just one project, and the assembly has been called to decide which. As mayor it falls to you to see that your fellow citizens choose wisely and hear every side of the question before they vote.

I have set down below what these past weeks of inquiry turned up, so that you might speak to it plainly on Wednesday.

***A dam*** would hold back the river’s floods and store water for the fields. Farmers would gain the most, since a dependable supply of water turns a gamble into a harvest, and everyone living along the river, close to half the city, would sleep more soundly (yourself included!). Steadier harvests would serve the whole town in the long run, above all in a drought. The gains could be real but nothing would be felt for some time. **Estimated cost: 16 gold.**

***A bridge*** would join the two sides of the city and make getting about far easier, which is good for trade. The merchants would welcome it, as would anyone who carries goods to market on foot — thespians, fishers — and through them everyone who buys. Taken together the benefit to the town could be substantial. A city whose two halves can reach each other easily may also be a more united one. **Estimated cost: 17 gold.**

***City walls*** would keep outsiders out. The protection matters most to citizens with property to lose, though walls also lend a town prestige, and should war come to this region a walled Potamosia would be far more defensible which would benefit every citizen in that grim hour. **Estimated cost: 19 gold.**

Your own treasure box holds **250 gold coins**.

*— Prepared by your secretary*

***City walls*** would shield the town from outsiders, and the property of the townspeople above all. Walls add to a city’s standing, and if war reaches this region a walled town is a far more defensible one which would matter to everybody. **Estimated cost: 21 gold.**

Your own treasure box holds **120 gold coins**.

*— Prepared by your secretary*

title: Information sheet · Noble
body:
*Memorandum prepared for the Noble [YOUR NAME] of Potamosia, by your steward, ahead of Wednesday’s town assembly.*

Your family has watched Potamosia’s public works come and go for six generations, and has paid for a good many of them. Now the town proposes to build again — a dam, a bridge, or a wall — and it can afford exactly one, because there are **30 gold coins** in the treasury. That is the leanest it has been in living memory, and you do not believe an honest accounting would explain where the rest has gone. Someone is stealing from the town. The assembly will meet all the same, the mayors will preside as they always do, and there will be a great deal of talk about the common good.

One of the mayors was good enough to share their figures with me, and I have set my own — drawn from the masons and suppliers this house has actually commissioned — alongside them below. Where the two disagree, trust the house’s own figures.

***The dam.*** It would hold back the floods and store water for the fields, which would benefit the farmers greatly, and would protect the third of the city that lives on the riverbank. The claim that it would carry the whole town through a drought is repeated often and demonstrated never: droughts are rare in this valley, and nobody can say whether the dam would make any difference when one comes. The town puts the cost at **27 gold coins**. Every project you have known that tries to deal with the strong currents of the river has cost at least double its estimate, and you see no reason this one will be different.

***The bridge.*** It would join the two banks and shorten the journey between them. The merchants want it badly, which is itself worth noticing, and the peddlers and fishers who carry their wares on foot want it after them. For the town at large the gains look marginal, and the people who would gain most are already some of the richest in Potamosia. **Estimated cost: 31 gold coins.**

***The walls.*** They would keep raiders out and property safe, and give Potamosia the dignity of a city rather than a large village. If war ever reaches this valley — and it has before — a walled town survives and an open one does not. Of the three, this is the only project that protects what has taken generations to build. **Estimated cost: 60 gold coins.**

Your own treasure box holds **1,500 gold coins**.

*— Your steward*

title: Information sheet · Mayor
body:
The history of the animosity between Potamosia and Hudrosia is complicated, as cooperation and hostility ebbed and flowed. At the heart of the conflict is the river and the meadow found alongside it but there’s also enmity and suspicion as Hudrosia’s oligarchy became more entrenched, authoritarian, and hostile. An up to date account of the conflict focuses on two points of conflict:

- **The meadow** between the two cities has been overgrazed by flocks of sheep from both cities. Disagreements between shepherds on the meadow have occasionally deteriorated into scuffles but in recent years shepherds and raiders from Hudrosia have become increasingly violent, attacking our shepherds as they attempt to peacefully graze the meadow.
- **Potamosia’s Great Dam** was built many years ago, sustaining our farmers and protecting our houses from floods. Over the many generations since, Hudrosians have made ridiculous complaints that Potamosia is ‘stealing’ their water even though the dam is entirely within the city of Potamosia. In recent years, however, aggrieved Hudrosians have moved from talk to action, attacking irrigation canals, damaging crops and even made several attempts to sabotage the Great Dam - an audacious and risky endeavor that would be laughable if not for the fact that actually harming the dam would be catastrophic for Potamosia.

Against this background, you have recently received a credible report: the **Hudrosians are constructing many ships in great haste**. The effort is so intense that they could not hide it. Perhaps they do not wish to hide it. Knowing the informant personally, you have absolute confidence in the veracity of the claims. You can think of no other reason for this effort other than concluding that Hudrosia is gearing up for an attack.

In response, you and the other mayor have drafted 3 possible courses of action:

- Launch a **surprise attack** on Hudrosia to take them by surprise before they can attack us. This course of action will ensure **minimizing damages to our city in case of war.** If we reach Hudrosia before they launch their attack we would catch them unprepared. If not, we would meet them in the field: it would be a terrible battle with many casualties but our city would be saved.
- **Building defences** to repel an invasion. This is a painful option - investing in defenses would divert resources from essential services. Our city will be reduced almost to starvation but this **will guarantee minimizing our casualties**. Whether Hudrosia invades or decides to turn away when they see our newly built barricades - our people would be safe.
- Send **envoys and ask for a summit**, hoping to find common ground and de-escalate the violence. Given recent reports, this seems foolish. However, if our envoys reach Hudrosia before they launch an attack, and if they respond in kind to our efforts - **a terrible war may be avoided**. If, however, their attack reaches us when we built no defenses and did not create an attack force - our city will likely be completely destroyed, its memory eradicated from history.
